explanation: Fires on a middle subword piece inside a long word that has been split into several tokens, mostly in non-English text (Turkish, German, Romanian, Czech, Hindi) or in Latin/technical names (Rattus norvegicus, echocardiography, Marburg). The strongest case is a Turkish suffix piece; English function words and whole words give little or nothing.

Fires on the second or later token of a multi-token technical term or fixed phrase, where the earlier tokens make the continuation predictable (cyclo-pro-panation, dehydro-gen-ase, Emit-ting, J. Org. Chem, Series B round, Scopes Trial, pulse pressure, regress to the mean). It fires strongly across chemistry, medicine, finance and code. Generic function words outside such phrases give weak activation.

Mixed. The clearest pattern is 'Biography' (and 'Folklore') as a section heading right after a one-line Wikipedia-style bio intro. Other strong examples are a word completing a slogan, title or headline phrase (Your success, The Solution, The Hill, Deal Score, Wishlist Action). Some examples do not fit either pattern.

Fires on function words and structural tokens in formulaic or boilerplate positions. Examples: 'the' right after a transitive verb in scientific abstracts ('suppressed the', 'mediate the', 'induced the'), 'and'/'of'/'with' in license headers, the 'function' keyword starting a JS definition, and punctuation such as ':' or '.)' before list items or equations. The token itself is usually generic; what drives it is a predictable syntactic slot.

Fires on a broad mix of tokens: code comment markers ('//', '<!--'), SQL keywords (INTO, TRIGGER), compound-word continuations (gram-negative, host-environment, Structured), and nouns inside noun phrases (Game of the Year, second season). No single shared trigger is visible.

Fires on many unrelated tokens: identifier pieces in code (emptyOnRead, jsToolBar.strings), medical subword pieces (debridement, cruciate, melanoma), pronouns ('I', 'they'), sentence starts ('But'), and repeated list-like nouns (family singing, Onsite Service). No consistent context or token type is apparent.

Fires on the digit token '6' inside a number, especially the decade/century digit of a year (1631, 1967, 1968, 1861) and digits in zip codes, ports and decimals. It is weaker for '6' in citation or patent numbers and moderate for the word 'six'. Other digits and non-numeric tokens do not fire.

Fires on the first token of a defined short name inside quoted or parenthesized definitions: most strongly 'License' in '(the "License")' in license headers, and also legal short-form names ('("GE")', '("Cooley")', nickname quotes like Daniel "Danny"). It fires moderately on acronym definitions in parentheses after a spelled-out term, e.g. 'bone marrow (BM)'.

Fires on the punctuation and newline that end a title, question or abstract and lead into the body: '?

' after a Q&A title, '.'
' closing a quoted arXiv abstract, '{
' opening a block, or 'How' starting the question body. Punctuation and newlines in the middle of running text are weak.

Fires on a broad mix: uppercase subword pieces in legal headers (MEM-ORANDUM, J-UD-GMENT), 'of' in organization or rule names, code punctuation (':', 'endif', '$'), and assorted word pieces. No clear shared trigger.

Fires on separators and connectives in lists of names or place descriptions: commas and 'and' between place names, 'of'/'on'/'to' after place-type nouns (village of, parish of, licensed to), newlines between commune names, and the opening quote of a string value in a JS object list. It is mostly tied to geographic or proper-name listing contexts.

Fires on the second or later token of established technical or statistical terms (likelihood ratio, Cox proportional hazards, principal component, gel permeation chromatography, tissue microarray, slow wave). It also fires on code tokens such as '<' after an interface name, 'STAThread' and 'argc'. Science-methods vocabulary dominates; the code cases are a looser second group.

Fires mostly on digits inside numbers that sit in citation keys ([@b3], [@pone.0099234]), years, math problems and code constants, and also on a few code/import tokens and odd subwords. Digits mid-number are the main trigger; the rest are scattered.

Fires on physics and condensed-matter vocabulary, especially 'metal'/'metallic', 'ground' (state), lattice and networks, in solid-state or quantum physics prose. It also fires on LaTeX math-markup tokens ('{', '\text', '\limits'). Physics/math technical context is the common thread.

Fires on a middle word piece of a word broken into rare fragments, often all-caps or legal-heading words (RE-HE-ARING, THEM-SEL-VES, Share-Alike) or proper names (Gayathri, Burtschy). It also fires on 'at' in technical-patent position phrases ('at right angles', 'at a position'). Mostly tokenization-fragment driven, with a separate 'at' group.

Fires most strongly on 'software' in 'This program is free software' / 'Free Software Foundation' license text. Elsewhere it fires on mid-word pieces of uncommon words (equestrians, denatured, crocodiles, Doppler, Auto-generated). These two groups do not obviously relate.

Fires on the first digit of a number right after a minus sign (e.g. '-1' in '-108', '-3/4', '-7*o'), most strongly in generated arithmetic/algebra problems. It also fires on the comma in diff hunk headers ('@@ -2912,7'). Numbers without a preceding minus are weak.

Fires on a heterogeneous set of tokens in news and casual prose: 'workers' after a count, last pieces of names (Cantor, Proffitt, Foles), trailing zeros of money amounts, pronouns or verbs completing a phrase. No coherent shared feature.

Fires on the second word of common fixed multiword expressions where the continuation is highly predictable: 'feel free', 'of course', 'most common', 'only supposed', 'at first', 'as published', 'names of its contributors', 'NONPRECEDENTIAL'. It is weak when the continuation is not formulaic.

Fires on predictable continuation tokens in a scattered set of contexts: word endings in chemistry or medicine terms (arachid-onic, eicosapentaeno-ic, opiate withdrawal), citation and section ID digits (#s0005, bib0015), legal reporter abbreviations (Ill., Cal.App), and phrases like 'for Best Picture' and 'master's degrees'. The contexts do not share a theme.

Fires on nouns naming a service, business or profession in commercial or marketing text (audit market, SEO company, services, Plumbing, professionals, repairs, Surgery). It fires more weakly on law-firm names in legal citations. Non-commercial uses of words are weak.
